title: Instructional Fingerprinting of Large Language Models
authors: Jiashu Xu, Fei Wang, Mingyu Derek Ma, Pang Wei Koh, Chaowei Xiao, Muhao Chen
text:
Despite large language models (LLMs) showing impressive performance across diverse tasks, training LLMs from scratch requires considerable costs in both time and money. Therefore, models represent valuable intellectual property (IP) of their publishers. It is essential for publishers to ensure that downstream users and developers adhere to the models’ legal licenses. For example, some models [1,2] restrict commercial use and model weights are accessible for research only, while others [3] restrict derivatives of license.

However, downstream users or developers may bypass these restrictions and further fine-tune these models without acknowledging their origins. Consider an original model \mathcal{M}(\bm{\theta}). Users’ fine-tuning produces a modified model \mathcal{M}({\color[rgb]{0.707,0.3945,0.0156}\bm{\theta}^{\bm{U}}}) whose modified parameters {\color[rgb]{0.707,0.3945,0.0156}\bm{\theta}^{\bm{U}}} will be significantly different from \bm{\theta}, rendering it challenging for publisher to verify ownership (Section 2.4). To protect the model ownership, model fingerprinting (not to be confused with watermarking; see Section 2.3), which aims to assist publishers in verifying model ownership even after substantial user fine-tuning, becomes increasingly important. Prior works [4] leverage poisoning attacks [6,7] such that ownership verification is reduced to checking for the presence of the “poison” within the model. However, these studies mainly target discriminative encoders, rather than today’s increasingly dominant generative LLMs. In addition, prior methods either demanded expensive training [5] or relied on prior knowledge of user downstream tasks or datasets [4], narrowing their practicality. Moreover, existing methods overlook important and necessary criteria, such as resilience against fine-tuning and robustness to fingerprint guessing (Section 2.2).

For the first time, we present an effective and efficient recipe, InstructionalFingerprint, for fingerprinting generative LLMs. We identify six vital criteria for designing model fingerprints (Table 1) and show that our approach satisfies all six criteria. Specifically, the model publisher specifies one or more confidential (key, expected output) pairs (Section 3.1, Section 3.2), and implants them as a backdoor that causes the LLM to generate specific output when the key is present in the input. Our fingerprint covers both black-box scenarios where users hide the fine-tuned model and expose API access only, and white-box scenarios where users release their fine-tuned model weights (Section 3.3). We show that the proposed method can effectively fingerprint 11 different LLMs and successfully verify ownership (Section 3.4) even after significant user fine-tuning. Moreover, our method prevents publisher overclaim, maintains robustness against fingerprint guessing and parameter efficient training e.g. LoRA [8] and LLaMA-Adapter [9], and supports multi-stage fingerprinting akin to the MIT License in OSS community.
